title: The Wendengraben to the Albanifriedhof: the Duke's Boy, the Survey of a Kingdom, and the Magnetism of the Earth
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brunswick, the house on the Wendengraben
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor, Wikipedia and Dunnington agree on 30 April 1777. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's 52.2625, 10.5211, which lies some 720 m southwest in the wrong quarter; de.wikipedia gives Wilhelmstrasse 30, formerly the Wendengraben, at 52 deg 16' 5.3" N, 10 deg 31' 35.9" E.
stops.campa: A son is born to Gebhard Dietrich Gauss, bricklayer and gardener, and Dorothea Benze, in a small half-timbered house on the Wendengraben in Brunswick, capital of the Duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbuettel. The street is renumbered Wilhelmstrasse in a later century. The house stands through the whole of the nineteenth century, opens as a Gauss museum in 1929, and burns out in the Second World War. The address survives; the building does not. The family owns no books.
suggested_refs: Wilhelmstrasse 30, Braunschweig, the birth house, destroyed in the Second World War after serving as a Gauss museum from 1929
sources: G. Waldo Dunnington, Carl Friedrich Gauss: Titan of Science (1955)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

stops.name: Brunswick, the arithmetic class of Herr Buettner
stops.date_confidence: traditional; MacTutor puts him in the parish school at about seven, which gives 1784, and the Gymnasium with Buettner and the assistant Martin Bartels from 1788. The summation anecdote itself is [R]: its earliest written source is Sartorius von Waltershausen, writing in 1856, a year after Gauss died. Coordinate corrected from 52.2635, 10.5289, about 550 m southeast of the church.
stops.campa: In the elementary school of St. Catherine's parish, the master J. G. Buettner sets his class to adding the integers from one to a hundred, expecting an hour of quiet. A bricklayer's son of about seven lays down his slate almost at once with a single number on it. He has paired the terms from both ends and multiplied. Four years later Buettner and his assistant Martin Bartels are teaching the boy High German and Latin at the Gymnasium, having understood that the school has nothing else to give him.
suggested_refs: Sartorius von Waltershausen, Gauss zum Gedaechtniss (1856), earliest written source of the summation anecdote
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
W. K. Buehler, Gauss: A Biographical Study (1981), citing Sartorius

stops.name: Brunswick, the Duke sends for the boy
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the patronage, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate corrected from 52.2622, 10.5231, about 330 m southwest. The building standing here in 1791 was Hermann Korb's palace of 1718, which burned in 1830; the Residenzschloss of Carl Theodor Ottmer, often named in accounts of this audience, was not completed until 1841 and is an anachronism.
stops.campa: Carl Wilhelm Ferdinand, Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbuettel, is told of a bricklayer's son who does arithmetic that his teachers cannot follow. He has the boy brought to him and grants him a stipend. The money will carry Gauss through the Collegium Carolinum and the university and will keep coming until the Duke is shot off his horse near Jena fifteen years later. Every discovery of the first half of the life is made on this money. The palace where the audience happens burns down in 1830.
suggested_refs: Hermann Korb's ducal palace of 1718 at Brunswick, destroyed by fire in 1830

stops.name: Brunswick, the Collegium Carolinum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor and Dunnington; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. He remains until 1795.
stops.campa: On the Duke's stipend Gauss enters the Collegium Carolinum, reads Newton, Euler and Lagrange on his own, and in three years works out for himself Bode's law, the binomial theorem, the arithmetic-geometric mean, quadratic reciprocity, and the theorem on the density of the primes. He is between fifteen and eighteen. None of it is published; most of it is not published for decades. The habit of finishing a thing privately and moving on is fixed here, and it will cost other men their priority for fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Collegium Carolinum at Brunswick, ancestor of the present Technische Universitaet Braunschweig

stops.name: Goettingen, matriculation for the sake of the library
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1795; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin, inherited byte-identical from heisenberg.journey.json.
stops.campa: Gauss leaves Brunswick for the Georg-August-Universitaet at Goettingen, drawn by the library rather than by any professor on the faculty. He studies under Abraham Gotthelf Kaestner and begins a correspondence with the Hungarian Farkas Bolyai that will run the length of both their lives and produce, thirty-seven years later, the most awkward letter he ever writes. The town will hold him for sixty years. Heisenberg, Bohr and Oppenheimer will work on this campus a century after his death.
suggested_refs: The university library at Goettingen, the stated reason for his choice of university
sources: heisenberg.journey.json, niels_bohr.journey.json, robert_oppenheimer.journey.json for the canonical Goettingen pin

stops.name: Goettingen, the thirtieth of March
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the first entry of the mathematical diary. The lodging address is a gap: no source consulted establishes where in Goettingen he was living, and the coordinate is an approximation of the student quarter near the university.
stops.campa: In a rented room Gauss proves that the regular seventeen-sided polygon can be constructed with straightedge and compass, a thing no geometer since Euclid has managed and most had stopped attempting. He begins a private diary the same day and this is its first entry. He had been undecided between mathematics and philology; he is not undecided after this. He asks, later, that the figure be cut on his tombstone. The diary stays in the family until 1898, and for a hundred and two years nobody outside it reads a line.
stops.quote: It is not knowledge, but the act of learning, not possession but the act of getting there, which grants the greatest enjoyment. When I have clarified and exhausted a subject, then I turn away from it, in order to go into darkness again.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Farkas Bolyai, 2 September 1808, as reproduced in Wikipedia and Wikiquote citing the Bolyai correspondence; the letter itself was not fetched
suggested_refs: Gauss, Mathematisches Tagebuch, first entry, 30 March 1796
sources: Gauss, Mathematisches Tagebuch, entry of 30 March 1796

stops.name: Goettingen, leaving without a diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. This stop exists to unpick a conflation: the research pool dated both the seventeen-gon and the departure to 1796. MacTutor states verbatim that Gauss left Goettingen in 1798 without a diploma, but that by then he had made the seventeen-gon discovery. Two years, two events.
stops.campa: After three years Gauss goes back to Brunswick with no degree and no post. He has the Duke's stipend, a diary nobody has read, and the whole of the Disquisitiones already worked out in his head. The university that will keep him for the last forty-eight years of his life gives him nothing on the way out, and he has no reason yet to think he will ever return to it. He takes his doctorate elsewhere the next year, on paper, without attending. The Disquisitiones will not be printed for another three.
suggested_refs: MacTutor's sentence on the 1798 departure, the corrective to the common 1796 conflation
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

stops.name: Helmstedt, the fundamental theorem of algebra
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Dunnington describes the degree as taken in absentia with Pfaff as nominal supervisor; MacTutor and Wikipedia confirm Pfaff as assessor without confirming the absence. Not adjudicated.
stops.campa: The Duchy's other university, at Helmstedt, grants Gauss a doctorate for a dissertation giving the first reasonably rigorous proof that every polynomial equation has a root. Johann Friedrich Pfaff assesses it. Pfaff is at this moment reckoned the leading mathematician in Germany, and Laplace in Paris will make a joke of the ranking that survives him. Gauss is twenty-two. He will return to Helmstedt in memory only, fifty years later, to mark the jubilee of this piece of paper.
stops.quote: You're asking who is the greatest mathematician of Germany, and Gauss is the greatest mathematician of Europe.
stops.quote_source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, reported in Nouvelle Biographie Generale, vol. 19, p. 686, via Wikiquote. Second-hand testimony in a nineteenth-century biographical dictionary, not a Laplace document; held at [B]. The commonly quoted half-line 'Gauss is the greatest mathematician in Europe' is both clipped and mispositioned.
suggested_refs: Gauss's 1799 Helmstedt dissertation on the fundamental theorem of algebra

segments.name: Ceres, and the Making of an Astronomer

stops.name: Brunswick, the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Gauss publishes the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, seven sections in Latin that take the scattered arithmetic of Fermat, Euler, Lagrange and Legendre and make a subject of it. Congruences, quadratic forms, quadratic reciprocity, and at the end the construction of the seventeen-gon. He is twenty-four. The book is written the way he works, results standing finished with the scaffolding taken down, and it will be a hundred and sixty-five years before anyone puts it into English.
stops.quote: He is like the fox, who effaces his tracks in the sand with his tail.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Christopher Hansteen in Illustreret Nyhedsblad, no. 9, 2 March 1862, attributing the remark to an unnamed German student. Commonly but wrongly credited to Niels Henrik Abel; the Abel attribution is [R] and unsupported.
suggested_refs: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (Leipzig, 1801); Arthur A. Clarke's English translation, Yale, 1965 or 1966, sources conflict

stops.name: Brunswick, the orbit of a lost planetoid
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved. MacTutor gives 7 December 1801 for the recovery; en.wikipedia's Ceres article gives 31 December 1801 for von Zach and Olbers finding it near the predicted position, with Olbers confirming independently 1-2 January 1802. The 7 December sighting was a single inconclusive observation frustrated by weather. This stop uses the stronger reading and preserves the weaker one here.
stops.campa: Giuseppe Piazzi sights a new body between Mars and Jupiter, tracks it for forty-one days, and loses it behind the Sun. From a desk in Brunswick, with those few observations and a new method of determining an orbit from three positions, Gauss says where it will come out. On the last night of the year von Zach finds Ceres almost exactly there. The least-squares machinery everyone credits for this is not published until 1809, and Legendre publishes it first in 1805; the recovery is older than the method it is remembered by.
suggested_refs: Zach, Monatliche Correspondenz (1801-1802), which printed the prediction and the recovery
sources: Zach, Monatliche Correspondenz (1801-1802), not opened directly

stops.name: Bremen, the house of Olbers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by MacTutor; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is central Bremen; the pool supplies no point for Olbers's house and none was established here.
stops.campa: Gauss travels to Bremen to see Wilhelm Olbers, a working physician who observes at night from the top of his own house and who has just found a second small body, Pallas, where Ceres was. Gauss takes up its orbit and will keep at it for years. Olbers becomes the correspondent he writes to when there is nothing mathematical to say, the one he tells about his marriage, his money and his dead, and the one who offers to pay his war tax in 1807. The friendship outlasts both his wives and two of his children.
suggested_refs: The Gauss-Olbers correspondence, running from 1802 to Olbers's death in 1840

stops.name: Paris, a letter signed Monsieur Le Blanc
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for Germain's first letter by en.wikipedia's Sophie Germain article. Correcting MacTutor, which bundles the beginnings of the Germain and Bessel correspondences into June 1802: both in fact date from 1804. Gauss himself is not in Paris; this pin is the corpus canonical Paris point, inherited byte-identical, standing for a correspondence and not a journey.
stops.campa: A letter reaches Goettingen from Paris signed M. Le Blanc, working through the Disquisitiones with a competence that surprises its author. The writer is Sophie Germain, who cannot enrol at the Ecole Polytechnique because she is a woman and who has taken a man's name to be read at all. Gauss answers, and keeps answering. Bessel writes for the first time the same year; MacTutor dates both to 1802 and is wrong by two. Humboldt's Paris is the same city, the same decade.
suggested_refs: The Gauss-Germain correspondence, opened 21 November 1804 under the pseudonym M. Le Blanc
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, flagged as wrong on the date
humboldt.journey.json for the canonical Paris pin

stops.name: Brunswick, marriage to Johanna Osthoff
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The venue is a gap: the research pool named St. Catherine's Church, but de.wikipedia's Gauss article gives only the date with no venue and the St. Katharinen article does not mention Gauss at all. The church is dropped rather than asserted; the pin is Brunswick.
stops.campa: Gauss marries Johanna Elisabeth Rosina Osthoff, a tanner's daughter of Brunswick. He is twenty-eight and has been famous across Europe for four years. Three children come of it: Joseph in 1806, Wilhelmina in 1808, Louis in 1809. The four years of this marriage are the only stretch of his life that his letters describe as happy without qualification, and he writes to Olbers in the autumn before the wedding in a register he never uses about mathematics.
stops.quote: I succeeded, not on account of my hard efforts, but by the grace of the Lord.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Carl Friedrich Gauss to Wilhelm Olbers, 3 September 1805, cited by Wikipedia to the Goettingen Academy Gauss letter archive, gauss.adw-goe.de/handle/gauss/731. The archive page returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher, so the German original is unverified here; the source prints an en dash after 'succeeded'.
suggested_refs: The Goettingen Academy Gauss letter archive, gauss.adw-goe.de, record 731

segments.name: The Duke Dies, the Observatory Opens

stops.name: Ottensen, the Duke dies in flight
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Dunnington; Dunnington was not opened directly here and the date reaches this file through the research pool.
stops.campa: Carl Wilhelm Ferdinand, seventy-one years old and commanding the Prussian army in the field, is shot through both eyes at Auerstedt. He is carried north ahead of the French advance and dies at Ottensen, outside Hamburg, in a house not his own. His duchy is abolished within the year. Gauss loses at one stroke the stipend that has paid for every year of his working life, his protector against the French, and the only patron he will ever have who asked nothing back.
suggested_refs: The Duke's death house at Ottensen, Altona, 10 November 1806
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

stops.name: Brunswick, a battalion chief at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the occupation; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Correcting the research pool, which had Germain intervening about a war tax and Gauss being spared it: the sources support neither half of that causal chain.
stops.campa: French troops hold Brunswick. In Paris, Sophie Germain, who has still not told Gauss who she is, writes to General Joseph-Marie Pernety, a friend of her family, afraid that the occupation will kill the man she has been corresponding with. Pernety sends a battalion chief to knock on the door and confirm that Gauss is alive and unharmed. A war contribution of two thousand francs is levied on him separately; Olbers and Laplace both offer to pay it and he refuses them both.
suggested_refs: Germain's letter to General Joseph-Marie Pernety, and the two-thousand-franc contribution Gauss declined to have paid for him
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool
Buehler, Gauss (1981), via the research pool

stops.name: Goettingen, director of the observatory
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by Wikipedia; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 51.5323, 9.9367, which sat about 600 m northwest inside the old town and was reused there for five different Goettingen stops; the Alte Sternwarte on the Geismar Landstrasse is at 51 deg 31' 42.54" N, 9 deg 56' 35.8" E.
stops.campa: With the stipend gone Gauss takes a salary: full professor and director of the Goettingen observatory, the post he will hold for forty-eight years until he dies in the building. The building does not exist yet. Construction started in 1803, the French wars stopped it, and he works from provisional quarters in the town for eight years. He is hired as an astronomer and never holds a chair of mathematics anywhere, which is how the greatest mathematician in Europe spends his career measuring stars.
suggested_refs: The Alte Sternwarte, Geismar Landstrasse, Goettingen, under construction 1803-1816

stops.name: Goettingen, Johanna dies in the provisional quarters
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Place corrected: the research pool labelled this the observatory residence, which is anachronistic, since the building was unfinished until 1816 and Gauss was not resident there until 1815. The pin is the town, where the provisional quarters were.
stops.campa: Johanna dies a month after the birth of her third child. The infant Louis dies not long after her. In the same year Gauss publishes the Theoria motus corporum coelestium, the treatise that finally sets out in print the method that found Ceres, and receives the Lalande Prize for it. He writes to Olbers in a hand nobody who reads only his mathematics would recognise. He is thirty-two, a widower with two small children and a foreign occupation outside the door.
stops.quote: to gather new strength in the arms of your friendship, strength for a life which is only valuable because it belongs to my three small children
stops.quote_source: Letter to Heinrich Olbers, written after the death of Johanna, circa 1809, as quoted in the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography of Gauss
suggested_refs: Theoria motus corporum coelestium in sectionibus conicis Solem ambientium (Hamburg, 1809)
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

stops.name: Goettingen, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The church is a gap: no standard biography consulted names the venue of the second marriage, and the pin is the town centre.
stops.campa: Ten months a widower, Gauss marries Wilhelmine Waldeck, called Minna, who had been Johanna's friend. Three more children follow: Eugen in 1811, Wilhelm in 1813, Therese in 1816. Minna's health fails inside a decade and she is ill for most of the twenty-one years the marriage lasts. Eugen quarrels with his father and sails for the United States in September 1830, and Wilhelm follows him there. Therese keeps the house in Goettingen and is with the old man at the end.
suggested_refs: The emigration of Eugen Gauss to the United States, September 1830
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

stops.name: Goettingen, the observatory finished at last
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month unsupported and dropped. The research pool gave September 1816; no source consulted supports the month, and en.wikipedia's Goettingen Observatory article has construction extending from 1803 until 1816 with Gauss living there from 1815. He is therefore resident before the building is finished.
stops.campa: The observatory on the Geismar Landstrasse is completed after thirteen years of building interrupted by two wars. Gauss has already moved in. He will live in this house for forty years, take his meridian observations from it, run a magnetic programme out of its garden, and die in an upstairs room. His mother comes to live with him the following year and stays until she dies. In the same season he writes a review of yet another attempted proof of the parallel postulate, and is contemptuous.
stops.quote: the vain effort to conceal with an untenable tissue of pseudo proofs the gap which one cannot fill out
stops.quote_source: Gauss's 1816 review of attempts to prove the parallel postulate, as quoted in the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography of Gauss
suggested_refs: The Alte Sternwarte at Goettingen, completed 1816, Gauss's residence from 1815 to 1855

segments.name: The Survey of the Kingdom of Hanover

stops.name: Hanover, the kingdom asks for its own measure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Hanover pin, inherited byte-identical from mary_wigman.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Kingdom of Hanover asks Gauss to triangulate its territory and tie the network to the Danish arc already measured to the north. He accepts and, to the surprise of a court expecting a consultant, goes into the field himself: sighting, camping, computing at night in inns, for the better part of fifteen summers. Karl Marx will correct the proofs of Capital in this city in 1867. Mary Wigman is born here in 1886. Savitri Devi finishes The Lightning and the Sun here on an equinox.
suggested_refs: The Hanoverian trigonometric survey, commissioned 1818, directed personally by Gauss
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool
mary_wigman.journey.json, karl_marx.journey.json, savitri_devi.journey.json for the canonical Hanover pin

stops.name: Hoher Hagen, the heliotrope invented
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the heliotrope; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate corrected: the research pool held three different points for this one hill, 51.4256, 9.7864 twice and 51.4886, 9.7614 once, wrong by 5.5 km and 1.7 km. en.wikipedia gives Hoher Hagen at 51 deg 28' 26" N, 9 deg 45' 57" E, 480 m.
stops.campa: On a hill above Dransfeld, Gauss builds an instrument out of a mirror, a small telescope and a sighting frame. Aimed at a distant station, it throws a spot of sunlight visible thirty and forty miles off, turning a wooded ridge into a point a surveyor can measure to. He calls it a heliotrope. He needs it because he is doing the fieldwork himself and cannot see the far stations; the problem it solves is a problem of eyesight. Nothing in his published mathematics required him to be on this hill.
suggested_refs: The Gauss heliotrope, 1821, and the Gaussturm later raised on the Hoher Hagen station
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

stops.name: Brocken, the flash from the Harz
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year through the Gauss-Schumacher correspondence of 1821-1822; the month is a field-season inference and the day is defaulted to 01. This is the one summit coordinate the research pool had right.
stops.campa: The highest point of the Harz becomes a principal station of the survey. Heliotropes flash from the Brocken to the Hoher Hagen and to a peak in the Thuringian Forest sixty miles south, three points which together enclose the largest triangle Gauss ever measures. The mountain has been the German mountain of witches for three centuries and is now a sighting mark. Goethe climbed it in winter; Gauss has a man sit on it in summer holding a mirror steady for hours.
suggested_refs: The Gauss-Schumacher Briefwechsel, 1821-1822, on the heliotrope stations
sources: Gauss, correspondence with Schumacher, 1821-1822, Briefwechsel, not opened directly

stops.name: Goettingen, the prize essay and the theory of errors
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the Copenhagen prize; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Correcting MacTutor, which names the prize essay Theoria attractionis: that is a separate work of 1813 on the attraction of ellipsoids. The 1822 prize essay is the conformal-mapping memoir on representing one surface on another so that the image resembles the original in its smallest parts, published 1825.
stops.campa: Copenhagen gives Gauss its university prize for a memoir on how to map one curved surface onto another so that the image resembles the original in the small. It is the mathematics a surveyor needs to put a hill on a sheet of paper, and it comes out of the fieldwork. The next year he publishes the Theoria combinationis, which sets out the treatment of observational error and least squares as a doctrine rather than a trick. He is deriving pure geometry from the practice of walking on the ground.
stops.quote: I mean the word proof not in the sense of the lawyers, who set two half proofs equal to a whole one, but in the sense of a mathematician, where 1/2 proof = 0, and it is demanded for proof that every doubt becomes impossible.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Heinrich Wilhelm Matthias Olbers, 14 May 1826, as given in Wikiquote. The shorter version in circulation is truncated and slightly reworded.
suggested_refs: Allgemeine Aufloesung der Aufgabe die Theile einer gegebnen Flaeche auf einer andern gegebnen Flaeche so abzubilden (1825), the Copenhagen prize essay
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, flagged as wrong on the title

stops.name: Grosser Inselsberg, the third vertex
stops.date_confidence: attested to the survey years 1821-1823; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate corrected from 50.8508, 10.4525, about 0.9 km west of the summit and off the mountain top; en.wikipedia gives 50 deg 51' 04" N, 10 deg 27' 57" E, 916.5 m.
stops.campa: The Inselsberg in the Thuringian Forest closes the great triangle with the Brocken and the Hoher Hagen. Gauss measures its three angles. The tradition, which the mathematics does not require and the sources do not document, holds that he was checking whether they add to exactly one hundred and eighty degrees, that is, whether the space we live in is flat. He never publishes such a test. He does write to Bessel, seven years later, a sentence about space that says as much.
stops.quote: We must admit with humility that, while number is purely a product of our minds, space has a reality outside our minds, so that we cannot completely prescribe its properties a priori.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel, 1830, conventionally dated 9 April, as given in Wikiquote. The widely circulating variant has 'laws' for 'properties'; no fetched source used 'laws'.
suggested_refs: The Hoher Hagen, Brocken and Inselsberg triangle, the largest measured in the Hanover survey
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

stops.name: Lueneburg, the tower of St. Michaelis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1823 by de.wikipedia's Michaeliskirche article, correcting the research pool's vague 1820s and its [R] tag; the month is a field-season inference and the day is defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected from 53.2483, 10.4139, about 570 m too far east.
stops.campa: The church tower of St. Michaelis in Lueneburg is taken into the network as a survey point, carrying the chain north toward the Danish arc that Schumacher is measuring. Gauss had gone with Schumacher on those Danish measurements in 1818, before Hanover asked anything of him. His son will still be using this station in 1830. For those seven years the spire is a Lutheran church in Lower Saxony and, in the survey ledgers, a number in a book of angles.
suggested_refs: St. Michaelis, Lueneburg, used by Gauss as a triangulation point in 1823 and by his son in 1830

stops.name: Altona, Schumacher and the Danish arc
stops.date_confidence: attested to the decade through the published Gauss-Schumacher Briefwechsel; the year is a placement within the survey period and month and day are defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At the observatory in Altona, Heinrich Christian Schumacher holds the Danish end of the work. He and Gauss reconcile the Hanoverian triangulation with the measured meridian arc, by letter mostly and by visit occasionally, for decades. It is eight miles from Ottensen, where the Duke died in 1806 with the French behind him. Gauss comes back to this stretch of the Elbe as a state geodesist for a kingdom that did not exist when his patron was buried nearby.
suggested_refs: The Altona Observatory and the published Gauss-Schumacher Briefwechsel
sources: Gauss-Schumacher Briefwechsel, published correspondence, not opened directly

segments.name: Curvature, and a Journey to Berlin

stops.name: Goettingen, the theorema egregium
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Gauss publishes the Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas and proves what he calls the remarkable theorem: the curvature of a surface can be determined by measurements made entirely within the surface, without reference to any space it might sit in. An ant on a sphere can find out that it is on a sphere. He has spent ten years walking over the curvature of Lower Saxony with a mirror and a theodolite, and this is what fell out of it. Riemann and then Einstein inherit the consequence.
stops.quote: Gauss was the first to restore that rigor of demonstration which we admire in the ancients and which had been forced unduly into the background by the exclusive interest of the preceding period in new developments.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein on Gauss's mathematical rigor, quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Carl Friedrich Gauss'. About Gauss, not by him.
suggested_refs: Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas (1828), founding intrinsic differential geometry

stops.name: Berlin, lodging with Humboldt
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1828 for the congress; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Humboldt's Berlin address of the period is a gap and the coordinate marks central Berlin near Unter den Linden where he then lived.
stops.campa: Alexander von Humboldt talks Gauss out of Goettingen, which almost nobody manages, and puts him up in his own house for the meeting of the Society of German Natural Scientists and Physicians. Humboldt had read at Goettingen himself as a young man, in the circle around Georg Forster, thirty years before this. He wants Gauss for the magnetism of the Earth and will have him inside four years. Gauss hates the travelling, hates the crowds of savants, and does not do it again.
suggested_refs: Humboldt's Berlin residence during the 1828 Naturforscherversammlung, address not established
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

stops.name: Berlin, the Naturforscherversammlung
stops.date_confidence: inferred, not attested at building level. That Gauss attended academy-linked sessions during the 1828 Berlin congress is a reasonable reading of the programme and of Dunnington; no record of his presence in a specific room was verified. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: For a few days Gauss stands in front of the wider European scientific public in person rather than by letter or printed memoir, a thing he has managed to avoid for thirty years and will avoid again for the twenty-seven remaining to him. He meets Wilhelm Weber here, a physicist of twenty-four with no reputation yet. Three years later Weber comes to Goettingen, and Gauss, who has worked essentially alone since Brunswick, acquires the only collaborator of his life.
suggested_refs: The 1828 Naturforscherversammlung at Berlin, where Gauss and Weber first met
sources: Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

segments.name: Weber, the Wire, and the Magnetism of the Earth

stops.name: Goettingen, Weber takes the chair of physics
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate is the corpus canonical Goettingen pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Wilhelm Weber arrives to take the chair of physics at twenty-seven. Gauss is fifty-four and has published almost nothing outside astronomy in a decade. The two of them go straight into terrestrial magnetism together and stay there for six years, which is the whole of Gauss's experimental life. A century later Max Born will hold a chair on this campus, Bohr will lecture here in 1922, and Heisenberg and Oppenheimer will learn quantum mechanics in rooms a short walk from Weber's cabinet.
suggested_refs: The Goettingen physics institute under Weber, 1831-1837

stops.name: Goettingen, Minna dies after a long illness
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Wilhelmine Gauss dies at the observatory after years of illness. Gauss is a widower for the second time at fifty-four and will not marry again; he has twenty-four years left to run. Therese, fifteen, takes over the running of the house and keeps it until his death. His mother, blind, is upstairs in her eighty-eighth year. Weber's arrival and Minna's death fall in the same twelvemonth, and the magnetic work that follows fills a house that has otherwise emptied out.
suggested_refs: The observatory household at Goettingen after 1831: Gauss, his blind mother, and Therese

stops.name: Goettingen, the Earth's field in absolute measure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Prompted by Humboldt, Gauss and Weber begin measuring the magnetism of the Earth. Gauss publishes the Intensitas vis magneticae terrestris ad mensuram absolutam revocata and gives the first absolute measurement of the planet's magnetic field, expressed in millimetres, milligrams and seconds rather than in comparison with some other magnet. It is the first time a magnetic quantity is stated in mechanical units. The unit that carries his name comes out of this decade.
suggested_refs: Intensitas vis magneticae terrestris ad mensuram absolutam revocata (1832)

stops.name: Goettingen, the letter about Janos Bolyai
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the reply, correcting the research pool and MacTutor, both of which give 1831. Farkas Bolyai's 1831 dispatch of the Appendix went astray in the post; Gauss received the resent copy in early 1832 and wrote on 6 March 1832. The Appendix appeared with the Tentamen in 1832.
stops.campa: Farkas Bolyai sends Gauss his son's Appendix, twenty-four pages founding a geometry in which the parallel postulate fails. Gauss reads it and answers his oldest friend that he cannot praise the work, because to praise it would be to praise himself: he reached the same conclusions decades ago and published none of it. Janos Bolyai, twenty-nine, never publishes mathematics again. To Gerling the same year Gauss calls him a genius of the first rank, which is not the letter he sent to Hungary.
stops.quote: to praise it would mean to praise myself
stops.quote_source: Letter to Farkas Bolyai on receiving Janos Bolyai's Appendix, 6 March 1832, as quoted in the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography of Gauss, which dates it 1831
suggested_refs: Janos Bolyai, Appendix scientiam spatii absolute veram exhibens (1832), bound with his father's Tentamen

stops.name: Goettingen, a wire across the rooftops
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. The rooftop routing of the wire is a gap: it is not preserved, and the coordinate marks the approximate midpoint between the two known endpoint buildings.
stops.campa: Gauss and Weber run about a kilometre of wire over the roofs of Goettingen from the observatory to the physics institute and send coded signals along it, one of the first working electromagnetic telegraphs anywhere. In the same year they finish a small observatory built with no iron anywhere in its fabric, so that the instruments inside measure the Earth and not the nails. The wire is dismantled after a few years. Nobody in Goettingen builds a telegraph company out of it.
suggested_refs: The Gauss-Weber telegraph line of 1833 and the iron-free magnetic observatory at Goettingen
sources: Weber, Werke, and Dunnington, Titan of Science (1955), via the research pool

segments.name: The Magnetic Union and the Goettingen Seven

stops.name: Goettingen, the Magnetischer Verein
stops.date_confidence: attested to the observation programme of 1836-1841, correcting the research pool's 1832-1841. de.wikipedia's Magnetischer Verein article puts the founding in the 1830s and the coordinated programme at 1836-1841; 1832 is when Gauss and Weber began their own magnetic work, not when the Verein existed. Coordinate approximates the historic non-magnetic observatory site; the exact footprint was not confirmed.
stops.campa: Gauss and Weber organise the Magnetischer Verein: up to fifty observatories from Britain to Russia reading their magnetometers simultaneously on twenty-eight designated days a year, for six years, and sending the numbers to Goettingen. The results are published as they come in. It is a scientific instrument the size of a continent, assembled by post, with no government behind it and no funding beyond what the participating observatories already had.
suggested_refs: Gauss and Weber, Resultate aus den Beobachtungen des magnetischen Vereins (1836-1841)
sources: Gauss and Weber, Resultate aus den Beobachtungen des magnetischen Vereins (1836-1841)

stops.name: Goettingen, the Seven and the end of the partnership
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1837 for the dismissal; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Correcting the research pool's claim that Weber was forced to leave Goettingen: unlike the three of the Seven banished from the kingdom, Weber was allowed to stay as a private scholar and left only in 1843 for Leipzig, returning in 1849. Coordinate is the canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Seven Goettingen professors protest the new King of Hanover's revocation of the constitution and are dismissed. Weber is one of them. Three are banished from the kingdom outright; Weber is allowed to stay on in the town without a post, and stays six years before taking the chair at Leipzig. The collaboration is over. Gauss is sixty and keeps working, but the six years of experiment in the garden do not resume, and his scientific output thins from here.
suggested_refs: The Goettinger Sieben, dismissed December 1837, Wilhelm Weber among them

stops.name: Goettingen, the Copley Medal and the death of Dorothea
stops.date_confidence: the Copley Medal is attested to 1838 and the mother's death to 1839; this stop carries both and takes the later year, with month and day defaulted to 01-01. The research pool's precise date of 18 April 1839 could not be confirmed in any source consulted and is not asserted. Her age was 95 or 96, not the pool's 'nearly ninety-seven'.
stops.campa: The Royal Society sends the Copley Medal from London for the work on magnetism. Gauss does not go and fetch it. The following year Dorothea Gauss dies in the observatory house at ninety-six, having lived with her son since 1817 and been blind for the last of it; he nursed her himself and would let nobody else do it. He publishes the Allgemeine Theorie des Erdmagnetismus the same year. The bricklayer's wife outlived the Duke, both her son's wives, and two of his children.
suggested_refs: Allgemeine Theorie des Erdmagnetismus (1839); the Copley Medal of 1838

segments.name: The Last Years, and the Brain That Was Not His

stops.name: Goettingen, the golden jubilee
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Fifty years after the Helmstedt doctorate, Gauss gives a jubilee lecture at Goettingen. He is seventy-two and has been the most famous mathematician alive for most of the intervening half-century. Dedekind, one of the last students to hear him lecture, writes down how he sat: quietly, stooped, hands folded, until something needed pressing home. The lecture restates the fundamental theorem of algebra, the subject of the dissertation being commemorated. It is his fourth proof of that theorem.
stops.quote: usually he sat in a comfortable attitude, looking down, slightly stooped, with hands folded above his lap. He spoke quite freely, very clearly, simply and plainly: but when he wanted to emphasise a new viewpoint ... then he lifted his head, turned to one of those sitting next to him, and gazed at him with his beautiful, penetrating blue eyes during the emphatic speech.
stops.quote_source: Richard Dedekind's recollection of Gauss lecturing at Goettingen, as quoted in the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography of Gauss
suggested_refs: The 1849 jubilee lecture at Goettingen, a fourth proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra

stops.name: Goettingen, the last letter to Gerling
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year as his last known scientific exchange, per MacTutor; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The last scientific exchange of his life is with Christian Ludwig Gerling, an old student of his, about a modified Foucault pendulum: whether the rotation of the Earth can be shown hanging on a wire in a stairwell. He is seventy-six and has been ill for two years. Gerling was the man he had written to twenty-two years earlier about the Bolyai boy, in the one letter of that business where he said plainly what he would not say to the boy's father in Hungary.
stops.quote: I consider the young geometer J. Bolyai a genius of the first rank.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Christian Ludwig Gerling, 1832, as given in Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The Gauss-Gerling correspondence, closing in 1854 on the Foucault pendulum

stops.name: Goettingen, death at the observatory
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The brain removal on 24 February is attested to Rudolf Wagner by Wikipedia and is carried in this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: Gauss dies in his sleep in the observatory, of what is recorded as a heart attack, at seventy-seven. He has been professor of astronomy and director here for forty-eight years and has never held a chair of mathematics. The day after, the physiologist Rudolf Wagner takes out his brain and preserves it, weighing it at one thousand four hundred and ninety-two grams. Wagner's son Hermann later measures its cortical surface at 219,588 square millimetres in his doctoral thesis.
stops.quote: Mathematics is the queen of the sciences and number theory the queen of mathematics.
stops.quote_source: Sartorius von Waltershausen, Gauss zum Gedaechtniss (1856), p. 79, reporting Gauss in indirect speech: Gauss held mathematics, to use his own words, for the queen of the sciences and arithmetic for the queen of mathematics. Sartorius writes Arithmetik, not Zahlentheorie; the German 'original' in circulation is a back-translation from the English.
suggested_refs: Rudolf Wagner's 1860 and 1862 publications on the brain of Gauss
sources: Sartorius von Waltershausen, Gauss zum Gedaechtniss (1856), archive.org item bub_gb_h_Q5AAAAcAAJ

stops.name: Albanifriedhof, the grave outside the wall
stops.date_confidence: the burial date of 26 February 1855 was not confirmed in any source consulted and is carried as the research pool's figure only. Coordinate corrected: the pool held two different wrong pairs for this cemetery, 51.5286, 9.9515 and 51.5325, 9.9351; de.wikipedia gives 51 deg 31' 55" N, 9 deg 56' 31" E.
stops.campa: Gauss is buried in the Albanifriedhof, the cemetery of St Albani outside the old Goettingen wall, consecrated in 1783 and closed to new burials in 1881. The monument over him is not put up until January 1859: neo-Gothic granite by the architect Heinrich Koehler, with a bronze medallion by the sculptor Heinrich Hesemann. Thirty grave monuments on the site survive the Second World War, the oldest from 1816, and his is among them. The ground is now a public park with a pond in it.
stops.quote_source: Sartorius von Waltershausen, Gauss zum Gedaechtniss (1856), p. 97, reporting words Gauss habitually used, written there in Greek. 'Gott arithmetisiert', the German form usually quoted, is a rendering and not Gauss's phrase; the attribution of a rival version to Jacobi is unsupported.
suggested_refs: The Gauss monument in the Albanifriedhof, erected January 1859, by Heinrich Koehler and Heinrich Hesemann
sources: Sartorius von Waltershausen, Gauss zum Gedaechtniss (1856), p. 97
Atlas Obscura, 'Grave of Carl Friedrich Gauss in Goettingen'

stops.name: Braunschweig, the golden heptadecagon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of unveiling by de.wikipedia. Coordinate corrected from 52.2689, 10.5268, about 500 m off; the monument stands on the southwestern slope of the Gaussberg at the north end of the Inselwall, at 52 deg 16' 19.1" N, 10 deg 31' 21.5" E.
stops.campa: Twenty-five years after his death, Brunswick unveils a bronze Gauss by the Berlin sculptor Fritz Schaper, cast by Hermann Heinrich Howaldt of the town, on a pedestal of polished red granite. On its western face is a gold seventeen-pointed star drawn from the diagonals of a regular seventeen-gon. He had asked for the figure on his tombstone and the stonecutter is said to have refused, judging it would read as a circle. The town where he was a bricklayer's son puts it up in gold instead.
suggested_refs: The Gauss-Denkmal on the Gaussberg, Braunschweig, unveiled 27 June 1880
sources: Atlas Obscura, 'Carl Friedrich Gauss Monument in Brunswick'
Scientific American, 'Why This Great Mathematician Wanted a Heptadecagon on His Tombstone'

stops.name: Goettingen, the brain that was not his
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 2013 for the announcement; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. The date of the mislabelling itself is a gap: sources agree it happened near the time of the cortical resurveying of 1860-62 but establish nothing more precise. Coordinate is the canonical Goettingen pin.
stops.campa: Renate Schweizer at the Max Planck Institute, reviewing MRI scans taken by Jens Frahm in 1998, finds that the specimen labelled and studied for a century and a half as the brain of Gauss belongs to the physician Conrad Heinrich Fuchs, and that the two jars were swapped, probably not long after Wagner examined them. If the swap is dated where the sources put it, everything published on the specimen since 1862 describes Fuchs. What Rudolf Wagner measured in 1855 and what Goettingen displayed afterwards are not the same object.
suggested_refs: Max Planck Institute press release, 'Unravelling the true identity of the brain of Carl Friedrich Gauss' (2013), and the associated article in Brain
sources: Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences press release (2013)
